job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
*Issue-spotting analysis for counsel; several points would ultimately depend on implementing rules and judicial interpretation.*

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—10,000-ton safe harbor.** The definition reaches only recovery of **more than** 10,000 metric tons, leaving recovery of exactly 10,000 tons or less outside the prohibition unless the Secretary separately acts under subparagraph (B).

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel allocation.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide recovery among multiple vessels, each staying at or below 10,000 tons, even if the fleet collectively recovers far more.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Meaning of “per year.”** The bill does not specify calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12-month period. That creates uncertainty about when tonnage resets and whether operations spanning two years may recover nearly 20,000 tons in a short period.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Threshold-crossing ambiguity.** It is unclear whether only recovery after the 10,000th ton is prohibited, whether the entire year’s recovery retroactively becomes “commercial,” or whether liability begins only when annual totals can be established.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” is undefined.** The bill does not say whether recovery occurs when nodules are detached, lifted from the seabed, brought aboard, landed, or processed. Different system configurations could therefore avoid or delay the point at which statutory “recovery” occurs.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Mass-measurement uncertainty.** “Metric tons” is not defined as wet weight, dry weight, ore weight, or contained-mineral weight. Water, sediment, and waste content could materially change whether the threshold has been crossed.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Non-vessel recovery systems.** The definition requires recovery “by a single vessel,” potentially excluding fixed platforms, subsea storage systems, shore-connected equipment, or autonomous collectors if no particular vessel legally performs the recovery.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Collector-versus-support-vessel ambiguity.** Modern systems may use several collectors, risers, barges, and processing or transport vessels. The bill provides no method for attributing recovered tonnage among them.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Transshipment.** The bill does not address transfers between collection, processing, and transport vessels. An operator could argue that no single vessel recovered the full quantity attributable to an integrated operation.

10. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Exact depth boundary.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters is excluded because the bill applies only at depths “greater than 200 meters.”

11. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Depth measurement.** The bill does not specify whether depth is measured from mean sea level, the instantaneous surface, chart datum, or another reference point, or how operations crossing the 200-meter contour are treated.

12. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—“Seabed” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the term includes the subsoil, seamounts, hydrothermal deposits, continental shelves, buried resources, or material already detached or stockpiled underwater.

13. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—“Other mineral resources” is undefined.** The phrase could mean all seabed minerals or only resources similar to polymetallic nodules. That uncertainty is especially problematic because violations can carry criminal penalties.

14. **Sec. 2(1)(A)—Exploration and testing remain permissible.** Sampling, mapping, equipment trials, prospecting, and other exploration that does not exceed the quantitative definition are not prohibited, even if conducted in preparation for later commercial production.

15. **Sec. 2(1)(B)—The responsible “Secretary” is unidentified.** Unlike section 6, which expressly names the Secretary of State, section 2(1)(B) never states which Cabinet secretary may make the determination.

16. **Sec. 2(1)(B)—Standardless discretionary expansion.** “Risks … comparable” and “deep-sea ecosystems” are undefined, and the bill specifies no factors, evidence threshold, findings, procedure, or judicial-review standard. This invites vagueness, due-process, and potentially nondelegation challenges.

17. **Sec. 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or notice.** The bill does not require rulemaking, publication, hearings, advance notice, or prospective application. Regulated parties may not know whether an activity has become criminally prohibited until after the Secretary acts.

18. **Sec. 2(1)(B)—Scope of “any activity.”** Read literally, subparagraph (B) could cover research, fishing, cable installation, or other nonmining conduct presenting comparable risks, despite the defined term being “commercial deep seabed mining.” That mismatch makes the provision both overbroad and difficult to administer.

19. **Sec. 2(2)—Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, LLCs not treated as corporations, trusts, associations, federal corporations, and other common business forms.

20. **Sec. 2(2)—Foreign affiliates and subsidiaries.** A foreign-organized subsidiary is not a U.S. person even if wholly owned or controlled by a U.S. company. The bill contains no ownership, control, agency, facilitation, or anti-evasion rule attributing its conduct to the U.S. parent.

21. **Sec. 2(2)—Territorial entities.** “Corporation organized under the laws of a State” leaves uncertainty about corporations organized in the District of Columbia, territories, tribal jurisdictions, or under federal law, because the Act does not define “State.”

22. **Sec. 2(3)—5,000-ton vessel threshold.** A vessel of exactly 5,000 gross tons, or less, is not a “covered vessel” and consequently has no registration or reporting duty.

23. **Sec. 2(3)—Tonnage system unspecified.** “Gross tons” can be measured under different domestic and international conventions. The absence of a specified measurement regime permits inconsistent classification.

24. **Sec. 2(3)—“Equipped for” is vague.** The bill does not specify what equipment is sufficient, whether temporarily removed or modular equipment counts, or whether support, processing, and transport vessels are covered.

25. **Sec. 3(a)—Geographic scope of “in the United States.”** The phrase is not defined to address U.S. territories, territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the outer continental shelf, U.S.-flagged vessels, or U.S.-registered aircraft. This creates significant jurisdictional gaps for non-U.S. persons.

26. **Sec. 3(a)—“Engage in” is undefined.** The prohibition may reach only the entity actually conducting recovery, rather than investors, lenders, insurers, technology providers, charterers, customers, or U.S. parents that support a foreign operator. There is no express prohibition on financing, facilitating, directing, contracting for, or purchasing minerals from mining.

27. **Sec. 3(a)—No import or downstream prohibition.** The bill does not prohibit importing, possessing, processing, purchasing, or selling seabed minerals recovered by an unregulated foreign operator.

28. **Sec. 3(a)—No anti-circumvention provision.** The Act contains no rule covering nominal foreign operators, vessel leasing, contractual delegation, corporate restructuring, or operations designed to remain just below the numerical thresholds.

29. **Sec. 3(a)—Governmental and nonprofit operations.** Because “commercial deep seabed mining” is defined principally by quantity rather than profit motive, the provision may unexpectedly cover government or nonprofit activity above the threshold. Conversely, the word “commercial” could generate an argument that a commercial purpose remains independently necessary despite the quantitative definition.

30. **Sec. 3(b)—Grandfather clause is extremely broad.** Mining “conducted under an exploration license” issued before enactment is completely exempt, without limits on production volume, duration, vessel, technology, operator, or geographic area.

31. **Sec. 3(b)—No issuing authority specified.** The exemption does not say that the exploration license must have been issued by the United States, NOAA, or the International Seabed Authority. A facially valid license from another country—or potentially another governmental entity—could be asserted as sufficient.

32. **Sec. 3(b)—Exploration license used for commercial mining.** The provision expressly exempts “mining” conducted under an “exploration” license, potentially converting pre-enactment exploration rights into an unlimited commercial-mining exemption even where the license itself was not intended to authorize production.

33. **Sec. 3(b)—Validity and continuity omitted.** The bill does not require a grandfathered license to remain valid, active, compliant, or unexpired. It also does not address renewals, amendments, extensions, reinstatements, assignments, or successor licenses.

34. **Sec. 3(b)—Transferability ambiguity.** Nothing expressly limits the exemption to the original licensee. Operators could argue that the exemption follows the license, project, or mining activity after assignment, acquisition, or corporate reorganization.

35. **Sec. 3(b)—No scope limitation.** The exemption is not expressly restricted to the tract, work plan, equipment, recovery ceiling, or other terms existing on the enactment date. It could therefore protect materially expanded operations nominally conducted “under” an old license.

36. **Sec. 3(c)—Unbounded environmental-assessment exemption.** The bill imposes no quantity, duration, method, location, approval, or scientific-protocol limit on activities undertaken for environmental assessment. A large-scale operation could claim that recovery is needed to assess environmental effects.

37. **Sec. 3(c)—Subjective or mixed purpose.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, or require an independent agency to approve that purpose. An operation with both assessment and commercial objectives may therefore invoke the exemption.

38. **Sec. 3(c)—Disposition of recovered minerals.** Nothing prevents minerals recovered during an exempt assessment from being retained, processed, or sold. The absence of a sales or profit restriction creates a direct route for commercially valuable recovery under the exemption.

39. **Sec. 4(a)—“Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, management, operational control, and employment may be split among several entities, leaving uncertainty about who must register and who is liable for omissions.

40. **Sec. 4(a)—Registration has no jurisdictional nexus.** Read literally, “each covered vessel” includes foreign vessels and operators with no U.S. connection. Congress rarely can make such a worldwide administrative command effective without a clearer jurisdictional basis.

41. **Sec. 4(a)—No registration deadline or process.** The section does not say when registration must occur, what information must be supplied, whether NOAA may reject or cancel a registration, or whether NOAA may issue implementing regulations.

42. **Sec. 4(b)—Reporting requirements are indeterminate.** “Describing the recovery activities” supplies no mandatory data fields, measurement standards, locations, supporting records, or reporting format. Minimal narrative reports could arguably satisfy the text.

43. **Sec. 4(b)—Certification is undefined.** The provision does not say who must certify, what the certification must state, whether it is under penalty of perjury, or what knowledge and inquiry are required.

44. **Secs. 4 and 5—Registry duties are unenforceable under the stated penalty section.** Section 5 imposes penalties only for violations of section 3. No penalty, suspension authority, or other remedy is provided for failure to register, report, or certify accurately under section 4.

45. **Sec. 4—No confidentiality or disclosure rules.** The bill does not address whether commercially sensitive reports are public, protected, or subject to special treatment under FOIA. That omission may discourage detailed reporting and generate disclosure litigation.

46. **Sec. 5(a)—No penalty-assessment mechanism.** The Act does not identify an enforcing agency, authorize administrative assessment, prescribe notice and hearing procedures, provide judicial-review rules, or expressly authorize injunctions, vessel detention, forfeiture, or license revocation.

47. **Sec. 5(a)—Daily-violation calculation is unclear.** Because the underlying definition uses an annual tonnage threshold, it may be impossible to identify which “day” constitutes a violation. The provision does not say whether each vessel, activity, ton, or project constitutes a separate violation.

48. **Sec. 5(a)—Penalty criteria omitted.** The bill establishes only a maximum and supplies no factors for culpability, harm, ability to pay, cooperation, or prior violations. That invites inconsistent enforcement and challenges to penalty calculations.

49. **Sec. 5(b)—Criminal vagueness concerns.** Ten years’ imprisonment is attached to terms such as “recovery,” “per year,” “comparable risks,” “environmental assessment,” and “under an exploration license” without clarifying definitions. The rule of lenity would likely favor defendants where those ambiguities affect criminal liability.

50. **Sec. 5(b)—Meaning of “willfully.”** The bill does not state whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of the law, knowledge of the factual threshold, knowledge of a Secretary’s determination, or merely intentional conduct. This is especially consequential where coverage may arise from a later agency determination.

51. **Secs. 3–5—No explicit recordkeeping or inspection authority.** NOAA or another agency is not authorized to inspect vessels, audit tonnage, compel supporting records, install monitoring equipment, or preserve samples. Proving threshold and exemption issues may therefore be difficult.

52. **Secs. 3–5—No attempt or evasion offense.** The Act does not expressly prohibit attempted mining, concealment, structuring, false attribution of tonnage, or evasion of the per-vessel limit. General criminal statutes may sometimes apply, but they do not cure the substantive gap.

53. **Sec. 6—“Seek to negotiate” is largely unenforceable.** The provision requires effort rather than completion, contains no required negotiating partners, benchmarks, reporting obligation, or consequence for failure, and gives no standard for determining whether the Secretary complied.

54. **Sec. 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether an agreement must duplicate the thresholds, exemptions, jurisdiction, penalties, and duration of section 3 or merely pursue a similar policy.

55. **Sec. 6—Deadline ambiguity.** The Secretary must “seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months,” which could require only that negotiations begin by the deadline rather than that an agreement be reached.

56. **Sec. 7(a)—No required National Academies report.** The provision assumes a report but does not direct or fund the National Academies to prepare one, identify who requests it, prescribe its contents, or establish a deadline. The statutory mechanism for ending the prohibition early could therefore be unavailable.

57. **Sec. 7(a)—“Acting on” a report is unclear.** Congress could arguably act after merely receiving or considering a report, even if the report does not recommend ending the prohibition. The bill does not require the joint resolution to be consistent with the report’s conclusions.

58. **Sec. 7(a)—“Serious harm” is undefined.** The standard lacks geographic, temporal, ecological, probability, and mitigation criteria. Requiring a finding that mining can occur “without” serious harm may also be read as either an absolute zero-harm test or a more flexible risk-management standard.

59. **Sec. 7(a)—No expedited congressional procedure.** The bill supplies no prescribed resolution text, committee-discharge rule, debate limit, or privileged floor procedure. Any joint resolution would move under ordinary legislative rules and require presidential signature or a veto override.

60. **Sec. 7(a)—Ending section 3 does not end the registry.** An early joint resolution terminates only “the prohibition in section 3.” Registration and reporting under section 4 would apparently continue until the ten-year sunset, even though the prohibited activity had become lawful.

61. **Sec. 7(b)—Automatic ten-year sunset defeats the report condition.** Regardless of whether the National Academies studies the issue or Congress finds mining safe, the entire Act expires after ten years. The apparently science-based duration in subsection (a) therefore has no effect beyond that date.

62. **Sec. 7(b)—No express savings clause.** The bill does not state what happens to pending enforcement actions, unpaid penalties, reporting obligations, or investigations when the Act expires. The general federal savings statute may preserve accrued liabilities, but the omission invites litigation.

63. **Secs. 5(a) and 8—Enactment/effective-date mismatch.** Section 5 purports to cover violations “on or after” enactment, while section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. The better reading is that section 3 cannot be violated during that interval, but the inconsistent language creates avoidable uncertainty.

64. **Secs. 3(b) and 8—Different operative dates.** Grandfather status is fixed by the enactment date even though the substantive prohibition begins 180 days later. Licenses issued during that window receive no exemption, while operations under pre-enactment licenses remain exempt.

65. **Secs. 4 and 8—No transition mechanism.** Because the whole Act takes effect after 180 days and NOAA has no express rulemaking mandate, there may be no functioning registry, forms, or reporting system when duties first become enforceable.

66. **Act-wide—No express rulemaking authority.** The bill does not clearly authorize any agency to define technical terms, establish tonnage accounting, administer exemptions, create registration procedures, or coordinate enforcement. Reliance on implied or preexisting authority would be contested.

67. **Act-wide—No designated lead enforcement agency.** NOAA receives registrations, the unidentified Secretary makes risk determinations, and the Secretary of State negotiates internationally, but no official is assigned responsibility for investigating or enforcing section 3.

68. **Act-wide—No coordination with existing seabed-mining law.** The bill does not amend, suspend, or reconcile the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act or existing licensing and permitting duties. Agencies could remain authorized—or required—to process licenses for conduct that section 3 separately prohibits or exempts.

69. **Act-wide—No treatment of existing commercial permits or contractual rights.** Apart from the broad exploration-license clause, the bill does not address commercial recovery permits, pending applications, reliance interests, takings claims, or government contracts. That omission creates both litigation risk and uncertainty about preexisting authorizations.

70. **Act-wide—Arbitrary threshold distinctions.** The environmental rationale is not tied to why 10,000 tons, 200 meters, 5,000 gross tons, or a per-vessel rather than per-operator threshold was selected. The unexplained line drawing may weaken administration and support arguments that materially identical operations receive irrationally different treatment.
